newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Council mulls more money for BSE research.
newsitem.headline: Council mulls more money for BSE research.

text.p: Research Ministers tackled three main issues at their Council on Monday, namely extra funds for both the EU's current research programme and for mad-cow research and likely outlines for the next framework programme.

On the latter, a European Commission spokesman said that one of the issues raised was a concern by the Cohesion Funds countries -- Greece, Ireland, Spain and Portugal -- that planned emphasis on high-technology, cutting-edge technologies in the Fifth Framework Programme would be to their disadvantage.

The spokesman said that Research Commissioner Edith Cresson did not want the argument to develop into one of cohesion issues - which she sees as amply covered by other instruments -- versus research policy.

The Commission's July Communication, "Inventing Tomorrow" COM(96)332, set out three suggested priority areas for the programme. These are "Unlocking the resources of the living world and the ecosystem", "Creating a user-friendly information society" and "Promoting competitive and sustainable growth.
Monday's debate was a "very general roundtable" on the Commission's communication, the spokesman said.

He said delegations generally backed the idea that there be clearly defined priorities, albeit without agreement on which, that there be flexibility in the rules to allow for unforeseen research requirements and that there be closer coordination between other national and EU-level research activities.

"We will present a working document which is much more detailed than 'Inventing Tomorrow' before the end of the year. The formal presentation of the fifth progrmme will come during the Spring of 1997," the spokesman said.
On the question of increased cash for research into Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), research ministers would appear to have limited options for action.
Ministers' draft conclusions spoke of the need for research efforts and information exchange on BSE to be "significantly improved" and called on the Commission to make suggestions.

They also asked that the Commission report back in December on BSE-related research undertaken with the Fourth Framework Programme and that it reinforce its research activities in this field. Minister will discuss the point again in December on the basis of a Commission communication and a report on mad cow disease due to be presented to the Commission next week by the Swiss Professor, Charles Weissmann.

Weissmann, a leading BSE expert, was nominated by Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler in March to head a group of experts to look into the transmission of BSE to humans. His group was also asked to look into the control of BSE, to examine existing BSE research and to set priorities for future BSE research.

For its part, the Commission said an action plan for additional BSE research would need 50 million Ecus, 5 million for coordinating member state activities and the remainder to fund a call for proposals to support research projects.
One EU diplomat in Luxembourg played down any possibility of there being any more BSE-related funds available from the Fourth Framework Programme as currently funded.

"For that you need a Council decision but you would be opening up a Pandora's Box if you did. There's a very delicate balance between the funds allocated for the Fourth Framework Programme," the diplomat said.
Another avenue, the top-up funding of 700 million Ecus for the Fourth Framework Programme proposed by the Commission on February 2, was also unlikely to bear fruit.
"It's clear we are not going to get that money," the diplomat said of a decision which, in any case, lies with ECOFIN rather than research ministers.
The last option is for the Commission to propose a budget line for the money during negotiations over the 1997 budget, something the diplomat said might also find favour with the European Parliament.

The Commission spokesman said no decision had yet been taken although he said it was clear that more BSE research money was needed. He said there was no question of taking funds from health-related research money for diseases like Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome and cancer.
He said the proposal for top-up funds remained on the table as a possible source of money.
"If someone wants to bury the idea that's for the Council to do. It's up to the ECOFIN how much money we get," he added.
Aside from BSE research, the wider issue of top-funds for the Fourth Framework Programme won support from the Irish Presidency.
"The presidency has sympathy for the Commission's view on this matter," Irish Research Minister Pat Rabbitte told the Council's closing news conference.

But he added that for many member states, the time was "not yet ripe for a decision" onan delegation, meanwhile, announced that country's intention to put itself forward as a candidate site for the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER), a joint project between the EU, Japan, Russia and the United States.
